final_answer:
In an economic system where prices are set by voluntary exchange, the price of a good or service is determined by the balance between how much producers want to sell (supply) and how much consumers want to buy (demand). When more people want to purchase something (increased demand) and fewer producers are willing to sell it (reduced supply), the price tends to rise. Conversely, if demand decreases or supply increases, the price usually falls. This process naturally coordinates production and consumption, allocating resources to meet preferences while signaling producers to adjust output.

When a government intervenes by setting a maximum allowable price (a price ceiling) below the natural balance point, it disrupts this coordination. At the lower price, producers may find it unprofitable or unsustainable to supply the same quantity, reducing availability. Meanwhile, consumers, facing a lower price, may attempt to purchase more, leading to excess demand. This mismatch creates shortages, as the quantity available falls short of what is desired. Shortages can manifest as reduced quality, longer wait times, black markets, or rationing mechanisms. The intervention also distorts incentives, often resulting in inefficient outcomes compared to the system’s self-regulating adjustment.
